## Overview

Concentration-QTc (C-QTc) modeling is a standard pharmacometric analysis in
cardiac safety assessment. The ICH E14/S7B guideline recommends
exposure-response modeling as the primary analysis method for evaluating a
drug's effect on cardiac repolarization, measured through the QTc interval.

This scenario walks through a complete C-QTc analysis using an open-source
thorough QT (TQT) study dataset. We demonstrate how to:

1. Prepare ECG and concentration data for modeling
2. Fit a **linear** mixed-effects concentration-ddQTcF model
3. Fit a **nonlinear** Emax mixed-effects model
4. Compare models and extract clinically relevant predictions

The dataset comes from the PhysioNet ECG repository
([Johannesen et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.13026/C2HP4K)), a five-way
crossover TQT study in 22 healthy volunteers receiving ranolazine, verapamil,
quinidine, dofetilide, and placebo.

---

## Data preparation

### Download and inspect the raw data

The dataset is publicly available from PhysioNet. Each row is a single ECG
replicate; there are three replicates per time point per subject per treatment
period.

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
url <- "https://physionet.org/physiobank/database/ecgrdvq/SCR-002.Clinical.Data.csv"
raw <- read.csv(url)
str(raw)
#> 'data.frame':	5232 obs. of  32 variables:
#>  $ RANDID  : int  1001 1001 1001 ...
#>  $ EXTRT   : chr  "Ranolazine" "Ranolazine" ...
#>  $ EXDOSE  : int  1500 1500 1500 ...
#>  $ TPT     : num  -0.5 -0.5 -0.5 0.5 ...
#>  $ BASELINE: chr  "Y" "Y" "Y" "N" ...
#>  $ PCSTRESN: num  NA NA NA 524 524 ...
#>  $ RR      : int  902 883 806 875 837 ...
#>  $ QT      : int  400 400 386 369 368 ...
```

### Compute QTcF and ddQTcF

The Fridericia correction adjusts QT for heart rate:
QTcF = QT / (RR / 1000)^(1/3), where RR is in milliseconds.

The change-from-baseline ddQTcF is the analysis endpoint recommended by ICH
E14. For each subject and treatment period, we subtract the subject's
pre-dose baseline QTcF from each post-dose QTcF measurement.

```{r prep, eval = FALSE}
# Fridericia correction
raw$QTcF <- raw$QT / (raw$RR / 1000)^(1/3)

# Average triplicate ECGs at each time point
agg <- aggregate(
  cbind(QTcF, PCSTRESN) ~ RANDID + EXTRT + EXDOSE + TPT + BASELINE +
    SEX + AGE + WGHT,
  data = raw,
  FUN = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  na.action = na.pass
)

# Compute per-subject, per-period baseline QTcF
baselines <- agg[agg$BASELINE == "Y",]
bl_avg <- aggregate(QTcF ~ RANDID + EXTRT, data = baselines, FUN = mean)
names(bl_avg)[3] <- "BL_QTcF"

# Merge baseline and compute ddQTcF
agg <- merge(agg, bl_avg, by = c("RANDID", "EXTRT"))
agg$ddQTcF <- agg$QTcF - agg$BL_QTcF
```

### Prepare the modeling dataset

We focus on dofetilide, the positive control in TQT studies and a classic
hERG channel blocker. Only post-dose records with measured plasma
concentration are retained.

```{r filter, eval = FALSE}
# Filter: dofetilide, post-dose, non-missing concentration
dof <- agg[agg$EXTRT == "Dofetilide" &
           agg$BASELINE == "N" &
           !is.na(agg$PCSTRESN),]

# Concentration is in pg/mL; convert to ng/mL for readability
dof$CONC <- dof$PCSTRESN / 1000

# Format for ferx: compartment-free model, all observations
ferx_data <- data.frame(
  ID   = as.integer(factor(dof$RANDID)),
  TIME = dof$TPT,
  DV   = dof$ddQTcF,
  MDV  = 0,
  CONC = dof$CONC,
  SEX  = ifelse(dof$SEX == "F", 1, 0),
  AGE  = dof$AGE,
  WGHT = dof$WGHT,
  BL_QTCF = dof$BL_QTcF
)

# Sort by ID and TIME
ferx_data <- ferx_data[order(ferx_data$ID, ferx_data$TIME),]

# Write CSV
write.csv(ferx_data, "dofetilide_qtc.csv", row.names = FALSE)
head(ferx_data)
#>   ID TIME       DV MDV   CONC SEX AGE WGHT  BL_QTCF
#> 1  1  0.5  -1.3827   0  0.120   1  25 54.8 395.1891
#> 2  1  1.0  12.1684   0  1.610   1  25 54.8 395.1891
#> 3  1  1.5  41.3927   0  1.930   1  25 54.8 395.1891
#> 4  1  2.0  47.3927   0  2.430   1  25 54.8 395.1891
#> ...
```

### Exploratory visualization

Before fitting, it helps to visualize the concentration-ddQTcF relationship.

```{r explore, eval = FALSE}
plot(ferx_data$CONC, ferx_data$DV,
     xlab = "Dofetilide concentration (ng/mL)",
     ylab = "ddQTcF (ms)",
     main = "Concentration-QTc relationship: Dofetilide",
     pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.5))
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
abline(h = 10, lty = 3, col = "red")  # ICH E14 threshold of concern
legend("topleft", lty = 3, col = "red", legend = "10 ms threshold (ICH E14)")
```

The scatter should show a positive concentration-ddQTcF trend for dofetilide.
The dashed red line marks the 10 ms threshold of regulatory concern from ICH
E14.

---

## Linear concentration-ddQTcF model

The simplest and most common C-QTc model is a linear mixed-effects model.
This is the standard approach recommended in the ICH E14 Q&A document and
most regulatory submissions.

The structural model is:

    ddQTcF_ij = intercept + slope * CONC_ij + eta_i + epsilon_ij

where `eta_i` captures between-subject variability in baseline ddQTcF and
`epsilon_ij` is the residual error.

### Model specification

Create a `.ferx` model file. This is a **compartment-free** model (no ODEs,
no dosing events) where the prediction equation defines the model directly,
analogous to NONMEM `$PRED`. Drug concentration enters via the `[covariates]`
block.

```{r linear-model-write, eval = FALSE}
writeLines("
[parameters]
  theta TVINTERCEPT(0.0, -50.0, 50.0)
  theta TVSLOPE(10.0, -50.0, 100.0)

  omega ETA_INTERCEPT ~ 100.0 (variance)

  sigma ADD ~ 100.0 (variance)

[individual_parameters]
  INTERCEPT = TVINTERCEPT + ETA_INTERCEPT

[structural_model]
  y = INTERCEPT + TVSLOPE * CONC

[covariates]
  CONC continuous

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD)

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  covariance = true
", "qtc_linear.ferx")
```

Key features:

- **Additive IIV** on the intercept (not log-normal, since ddQTcF can be
  negative).
- **Additive residual error**, appropriate for QTcF measurements in
  milliseconds.
- **`CONC`** is declared as a continuous covariate read from the data CSV.

### Fit the model

```{r linear-fit, eval = FALSE}
library(ferx)

fit_linear <- ferx_fit(model = "qtc_linear.ferx", data = "dofetilide_qtc.csv")
fit_linear
#> Model: qtc_linear  |  Method: FOCEI  |  Subjects: 22  |  Obs: 328
#> STATUS: CONVERGED   41 iterations   0.0s
#> OFV: 2086.7258    AIC: 2094.7258
#>
#> THETA
#> Parameter            Estimate           SE       %RSE
#> TVINTERCEPT        -13.076578     2.549766       19.5
#> TVSLOPE             29.580442     0.963271        3.3
#>
#> OMEGA
#>   ETA_INTERCEPT  [additive]  = 81.594  (SD = 9.03)  SE = 28.38
#>
#> SIGMA
#>   ADD  [additive]  = 13.643  (SD = 13.64, var = 186.14)  SE = 0.55
```

The slope estimate of ~29.6 ms per ng/mL is precisely estimated (%RSE 3.3%)
and confirms substantial QTc prolongation with dofetilide. The negative
intercept is expected: at zero concentration, ddQTcF should be near zero,
and the negative estimate reflects sampling variability.

### Regulatory prediction

A key deliverable in C-QTc analysis is predicting the ddQTcF at the
geometric mean Cmax of the therapeutic dose, with a two-sided 90% confidence
interval. If the upper bound of this interval exceeds 10 ms, the drug is
flagged for further evaluation.

```{r linear-predict, eval = FALSE}
# Extract estimates from the fit object
ests <- fit_linear$estimates
intercept <- ests$estimate[ests$param == "TVINTERCEPT"]
slope     <- ests$estimate[ests$param == "TVSLOPE"]

# Predict at a target Cmax (e.g. 2.0 ng/mL)
cmax <- 2.0
ddqtc_pred <- intercept + slope * cmax
cat("Predicted ddQTcF at Cmax =", cmax, "ng/mL:", round(ddqtc_pred, 1), "ms\n")
#> Predicted ddQTcF at Cmax = 2 ng/mL: 46.1 ms
```

---

## Nonlinear Emax concentration-ddQTcF model

When QTc prolongation plateaus at high concentrations, a nonlinear Emax
model better characterizes the relationship. This is common for hERG
blockers like dofetilide, where channel blockade saturates.

The structural model is:

    ddQTcF_ij = Emax * CONC_ij / (EC50 + CONC_ij) + eta_i + epsilon_ij

No intercept is needed in the Emax form because ddQTcF is zero when
concentration is zero by construction (the change from baseline at zero
exposure should be zero, with any residual offset absorbed by between-subject
variability).

### Model specification

```{r emax-model-write, eval = FALSE}
writeLines("
[parameters]
  theta TVEMAX(50.0, 1.0, 200.0)
  theta TVEC50(1.5, 0.01, 20.0)

  omega ETA_EMAX ~ 0.09

  sigma ADD ~ 100.0 (variance)

[individual_parameters]
  EMAX = TVEMAX * exp(ETA_EMAX)
  EC50 = TVEC50

[structural_model]
  y = EMAX * CONC / (EC50 + CONC)

[covariates]
  CONC continuous

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD)

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  covariance = true
", "qtc_emax.ferx")
```

The IIV on Emax is log-normal (the standard parameterization for a positive
parameter). EC50 is estimated as a fixed effect only; adding IIV on EC50 is
often not supported by the data in a 22-subject study.

### Fit the model

```{r emax-fit, eval = FALSE}
fit_emax <- ferx_fit(model = "qtc_emax.ferx", data = "dofetilide_qtc.csv")
fit_emax
```

### Model comparison

Compare the linear and Emax models by their objective function value (OFV)
and AIC. A lower AIC favors the more parsimonious model when both have the
same number of observations.

```{r compare, eval = FALSE}
data.frame(
  Model   = c("Linear", "Emax"),
  npar    = c(nrow(fit_linear$estimates), nrow(fit_emax$estimates)),
  OFV     = c(fit_linear$ofv, fit_emax$ofv),
  AIC     = c(fit_linear$aic, fit_emax$aic)
)
#>    Model npar      OFV      AIC
#> 1 Linear    4 2086.726 2094.726
#> 2   Emax    4 2166.958 2174.958
```

For dofetilide in this concentration range (0.04--3.3 ng/mL), the linear
model fits substantially better. The Emax model's `TVEMAX` estimate may
hit its upper bound, indicating that the data covers only the lower,
approximately linear, portion of a potential saturation curve. When a
nonlinear model reduces to a near-linear form but introduces estimation
difficulties, the linear model is preferred for both fit and regulatory
interpretability.

---

## Adding a Hill coefficient

If saturation is steep, the sigmoidal (Hill) Emax model adds flexibility:

    ddQTcF_ij = Emax * CONC_ij^gamma / (EC50^gamma + CONC_ij^gamma)

```{r hill-model, eval = FALSE}
writeLines("
[parameters]
  theta TVEMAX(50.0, 1.0, 200.0)
  theta TVEC50(1.5, 0.01, 20.0)
  theta TVGAMMA(1.0, 0.3, 5.0)

  omega ETA_EMAX ~ 0.09

  sigma ADD ~ 100.0 (variance)

[individual_parameters]
  EMAX  = TVEMAX * exp(ETA_EMAX)
  EC50  = TVEC50
  GAMMA = TVGAMMA

[structural_model]
  y = EMAX * CONC^GAMMA / (EC50^GAMMA + CONC^GAMMA)

[covariates]
  CONC continuous

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD)

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  covariance = true
", "qtc_hill.ferx")

fit_hill <- ferx_fit(model = "qtc_hill.ferx", data = "dofetilide_qtc.csv")
fit_hill
```

A `GAMMA` estimate near 1.0 suggests the standard Emax is sufficient;
values above 1.0 indicate steeper saturation.

---

## Covariate effects

Covariates commonly tested in C-QTc analyses include sex, baseline QTcF,
and body weight. This section demonstrates adding a sex effect on the slope
(linear model) and a baseline QTcF effect on the intercept.

### Sex effect on the linear slope

Women have longer baseline QTc intervals on average, and some drugs show
a sex-dependent C-QTc slope. We test this by adding a categorical sex
covariate:

```{r cov-sex-linear, eval = FALSE}
writeLines("
[parameters]
  theta TVINTERCEPT(0.0, -50.0, 50.0)
  theta TVSLOPE(10.0, -50.0, 100.0)
  theta THETA_SEX_SLOPE(0.0, -20.0, 20.0)

  omega ETA_INTERCEPT ~ 100.0 (variance)

  sigma ADD ~ 100.0 (variance)

[individual_parameters]
  INTERCEPT = TVINTERCEPT + ETA_INTERCEPT

[structural_model]
  SLOPE = TVSLOPE + THETA_SEX_SLOPE * SEX
  y = INTERCEPT + SLOPE * CONC

[covariates]
  CONC continuous
  SEX  continuous

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD)

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  covariance = true
", "qtc_linear_sex.ferx")

fit_linear_sex <- ferx_fit(
  model = "qtc_linear_sex.ferx", data = "dofetilide_qtc.csv"
)
fit_linear_sex
```

The `THETA_SEX_SLOPE` estimate quantifies how much the slope differs for
females (`SEX = 1`) compared to males (`SEX = 0`). A non-significant
estimate (relative standard error > 50% or confidence interval spanning zero)
suggests no meaningful sex difference.

### Baseline QTcF as a covariate on the intercept

Subjects with higher baseline QTcF may have different ddQTcF trajectories.
We can test this with a centered covariate on the intercept:

```{r cov-blqtcf, eval = FALSE}
writeLines("
[parameters]
  theta TVINTERCEPT(0.0, -50.0, 50.0)
  theta TVSLOPE(10.0, -50.0, 100.0)
  theta THETA_BL(0.0, -2.0, 2.0)

  omega ETA_INTERCEPT ~ 100.0 (variance)

  sigma ADD ~ 100.0 (variance)

[individual_parameters]
  INTERCEPT = TVINTERCEPT + THETA_BL * (BL_QTCF - 400) + ETA_INTERCEPT

[structural_model]
  y = INTERCEPT + TVSLOPE * CONC

[covariates]
  CONC    continuous
  BL_QTCF continuous

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD)

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  covariance = true
", "qtc_linear_bl.ferx")

fit_linear_bl <- ferx_fit(
  model = "qtc_linear_bl.ferx", data = "dofetilide_qtc.csv"
)
```

---

## Diagnostics

After selecting the best model, standard NLME diagnostics apply.

```{r diagnostics, eval = FALSE}
# Diagnostic plots (CWRES vs TIME, CWRES vs PRED, observed vs predicted)
plot(fit_linear)

# Numerical diagnostics from the sdtab
sdtab <- fit_linear$sdtab
head(sdtab)

# Conditional weighted residuals should be centered around zero
# with no trend over time or predicted values
plot(sdtab$PRED, sdtab$CWRES,
     xlab = "Population prediction (ms)",
     ylab = "CWRES",
     main = "CWRES vs PRED")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Individual predictions vs observed
plot(sdtab$DV, sdtab$IPRED,
     xlab = "Observed ddQTcF (ms)",
     ylab = "Individual prediction (ms)",
     main = "IPRED vs DV")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

---

## Extending to other drugs in the study

The same workflow applies to other compounds in the dataset. For example,
to analyze quinidine (a known QTc prolonger):

```{r other-drugs, eval = FALSE}
# Prepare quinidine data (concentration in ng/mL, no unit conversion needed)
quin <- agg[agg$EXTRT == "Quinidine Sulph" &
            agg$BASELINE == "N" &
            !is.na(agg$PCSTRESN),]
quin_data <- data.frame(
  ID   = as.integer(factor(quin$RANDID)),
  TIME = quin$TPT,
  DV   = quin$ddQTcF,
  MDV  = 0,
  CONC = quin$PCSTRESN / 1000  # ng/mL to ug/mL
)
quin_data <- quin_data[order(quin_data$ID, quin_data$TIME),]
write.csv(quin_data, "quinidine_qtc.csv", row.names = FALSE)

fit_quin <- ferx_fit(model = "qtc_linear.ferx", data = "quinidine_qtc.csv")
fit_quin
```

Verapamil is expected to shorten QT (negative slope) due to its combined
calcium- and hERG-channel blocking properties, providing a useful contrast.

---

## Summary

| Model | Parameters | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | intercept, slope, omega, sigma | Standard ICH E14 analysis; most regulatory submissions |
| Emax | Emax, EC50, omega, sigma | Saturating drugs (hERG blockers at high exposure) |
| Sigmoidal Emax | Emax, EC50, gamma, omega, sigma | Steep saturation requiring a Hill coefficient |
| + Covariates | + sex, baseline QTcF, weight | Subgroup differences and risk stratification |

All four models are **compartment-free** in ferx, meaning they use no ODEs
and no dose records. Drug concentration enters the model directly from the
data via the `[covariates]` block. This matches the analysis structure
recommended in regulatory white papers and ICH E14 Q&A guidance: the
concentration-QTc relationship is modeled as a direct regression, with the
PK model (if needed) run separately.

### References

- Johannesen L, Vicente J, Gray RA, et al. ECG data from the
  Concentration-QTc study. PhysioNet, 2014. doi:10.13026/C2HP4K
- ICH E14/S7B Q&A. Clinical and nonclinical evaluation of QT/QTc interval
  prolongation. 2022.
